# Distinct Radiation Responses in Virus-Positive and Virus-Negative Merkel Cell Carcinoma

**Authors:** Mona M. Ahmed; Hembly G. Rivas; Thomas C. Frost; James A. DeCaprio

**Affiliations:** 1Program in Virology, The Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## TO THE EDITOR

Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive skin neuroendocrine cancer (Ahmed et al., 2021). Nonviral MCC (MCCN) is caused by excessive exposure to UVR, whereas polyomavirus-associated MCC (MCCP) is caused by clonal integration of Merkel cell polyomavirus (Feng et al., 2008). MCCP tumors constitutively express the viral large T and small T antigens (Ahmed et al., 2021). TP53 is frequently wild type (WT) in MCCP and often altered in MCCN (Knepper et al., 2019).

Despite their distinct etiologies, MCCP and MCCN tumors have similar clinical features and treatment strategies (Schrama et al., 2011). MCC is managed by surgical excision followed by adjuvant radiation therapy (Bichakjian et al., 2018). Radiation therapy alone leads to survival rates similar to those of surgery (Patel et al., 2018). Radiation sensitivity has been shown to be associated with viral status in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (Rieckmann et al., 2013).

We assessed the sensitivity to ionizing radiation (IR) in the p53-mutant MCCN cell lines, MCC13 and MCC26, and the p53 WT MCCP cell lines, MKL-1 and WaGa (Houben et al., 2013). We considered MCC26 to be p53 mutant because it does not express p53 protein and because the DepMap portal reports damaging mutations in exon 3 of TP53 in this cell line (https://depmap.org/portal/). Cells were treated with increasing doses of IR, and cell viability was measured 3 days later. MCCP cells had a significantly greater viability decrease than MCCN cells (Figure 1a).

To determine whether cells underwent apoptosis after IR, cells were radiated and allowed to recover. All lines responded with the rapid appearance of phosphorylated KAP1, a DNA damage response marker (Figure 1b). MCCP cell lines upregulated the apoptotic markers, PUMA; cleaved caspase-3; and cleaved PARP. However, MCCN cell lines did not express these markers after IR. Levels of cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved PARP were significantly higher in MCCP than in MCCN cells, as measured by flow cytometry (Figure 1c). These results indicate that IR induced apoptosis in p53 WT MCCP but not in p53-mutant MCCN cell lines.

To determine whether IR-induced apoptosis required p53 activity, WaGa cells with doxycycline-inducible p53DD were treated with 5 Gy IR and harvested at 1 and 8 hours. Expression of p53DD did not affect checkpoint kinase 2 phosphorylation 1 hour after IR (Figure 1d). However, p53DD cells had reduced expression of p21, PUMA, cleaved caspase-3, and cleaved PARP relative to uninduced cells, indicating a requirement for p53 in apoptosis. To further address the role of p53, we irradiated MS-1 (p53-mutant MCCP) and UISO (p53 WT MCCN) cells (Houben et al., 2013). Although both p53 WT WaGa and UISO cells increased the expression of p21 after IR, UISO cells did not express PUMA and cleaved PARP (Figure 1e).

CDKN1A is a p53 target gene and contributes to a variety of cellular responses, including cell cycle arrest (Abbas and Dutta, 2009). To determine the effect of IR on the cell cycle in MCCN, MCC13 and UISO cells were pulsed with 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine to label cells in the S phase. After removal of 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine, cells were irradiated and allowed to recover. Without IR, MCC13 and UISO cells grew with similar kinetics (Supplementary Figure S1a). After IR, MCC13 and UISO cells progressed through the S phase, noted by a shift in 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine–labeled cells from 2 N to 4 N from 0 to 8 hours (Supplementary Figure S1b). Furthermore, irradiated MCC13 cells progressed through mitosis as indicated by the shift in 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine from 4 N to 2 N at 24 hours. However, the majority of irradiated UISO cells remained arrested at the G2/M phase (Figure 1f). WaGa cells, which express p21 and undergo apoptosis after IR, exhibited G2/M cell cycle arrest and an increase in sub-G1 cells at 24 hours after IR (Supplementary Figure S2).

To determine whether MCC cells could proliferate after IR, cells were counted up to 5 days after IR. The p53 WT MCCP cell line, WaGa, showed a significantly decreased cell number, reflecting its apoptotic response, whereas the p53 WT MCCN cell line, UISO, had a significantly reduced proliferation rate (Figure 1g). However, the p53-mutant MCCN cell lines, MCC13 and MCC26, continued to proliferate after IR. Irradiation slowed but did not inhibit proliferation of the p53-mutant MCCP cell line, MS-1.

To assess DNA damage signaling in MCC, cells were irradiated with 5 Gy and allowed to recover for 1 hour. All MCC cell lines rapidly activated DNAPK; the ATM target, KAP1; and the ATR target, CHK1(Figure 2a).MCC cells also expressed the double-stranded DNA break marker γ-H2AX after irradiation (Supplementary Figure S3a).

To determine whether MCC cells preferentially used distinct double-stranded DNA break repair pathways, cells were stained for RAD51, required for DNA strand invasion during homologous recombination (HR) (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010). MCCP cells had significantly more RAD51 foci after IR than MCCN cells (Figure 2b and c and Supplementary Figure S3b). Furthermore, RAD51 foci persisted in MCCP cells 24 hours after IR. The higher levels of HR repair observed in MCCP cells were not due to a larger S phase population (Supplementary Figure S4b and c).

To measure repair by nonhomologous end joining after IR, we assessed the presence of foci corresponding to phosphorylated 53BP1. Phosphorylation of 53BP1 is required for inhibition of end resection and promotion of nonhomologous end joining (Daley and Sung, 2014). Three hours after 5 Gy IR, a total of 53BP1 formed foci in all MCC cells that appeared similar in brightness and quantity (Supplementary Figure S3d). However, phosphorylated 53BP1 foci were brighter and more numerous in MCCN cells than in MCCP cells (Figure 2d and Supplementary Figure S3c). MCC26 cells had a significantly greater number of phosphorylated 53BP1 foci per cell than MCCP cells (Figure 2e). MCC13 cells also had a greater number, albeit not significant, of phosphorylated 53BP1 foci per cell than MCCP cells. Similar results were observed by western blot 1 hour after 5 Gy IR (Figure 2f). These results indicate that MCCN cells preferentially favored nonhomologous end joining repair, whereas MCCP cells used HR.

In conclusion, we identified p53 status as a predictor of radiation sensitivity in MCC. IR induced a p53-dependent apoptotic response in p53 WT MCCP cells, whereas p53 WT MCCN cells displayed cell cycle arrest and cell growth inhibition. p53-mutant MCCN cells remained capable of proliferation after IR. Although we showed that viral and p53 statuses influence the apoptotic response to IR in MCC cells, this decision may also be impacted by other factors, such as expression levels and activity of Bcl-2 proteins (Verhaegen et al., 2014). We also showed that MCCN cells had evidence of reduced levels of HR compared with MCCP cells after IR, consistent with the reports of HR-related mutations in MCCN (Cohen et al., 2016; Starrett et al., 2017). Although p53-mutant MCCN cells progressed through the cell cycle after IR, it is unclear whether the DNA damage was repaired before bypassing the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint. A limitation of this study is that MCC26, MCC13, and UISO cells have been classified as variant MCC lines and may not be representative of MCC tumors (Daily et al., 2015). In addition, cells received a single dose of irradiation, with the possibility that p53 mutant MCC cells may be sensitive to fractionated radiotherapy.
